title: Flightline Codebase Audit
scope: Worked example with four findings taken from the full audit. The audit was read-only. It covered security and data, logic and errors, and a live walkthrough of the UI on the seeded CSG-8 tenant.

findings.statusNote: Fixed: unique index migration 0114 + Manage Server proof.
findings.title: Any tenant could claim any Discord server (guild) ID
findings.summary: A tenant admin could type in the ID of a Discord server they do not run. The shared bot then showed that server's members and emoji to the wrong tenant.

evidence.excerpt:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "social_provider_configurations_provider_guild_unique"
  ON "social_provider_configurations"
  USING btree ("provider", ("configuration" ->> 'guildId'))
  WHERE ("configuration" ->> 'guildId') IS NOT NULL;
evidence.note: The fix: one Discord server can now belong to only one tenant.
If two tenants already share a server, the migration stops with an error. It does not pick a winner on its own.
Saving a new server ID now needs a matching proof from the same user.
The proof asks Discord for the user's servers. The user must own the server or hold Manage Server or Administrator.
Test: a server already bound to another tenant is rejected, even if that binding is disabled.

current.description: At the audit commit `dcebf31`, `saveSocialProviderConfiguration` stored any well-formed server ID. There was no proof of control and no uniqueness rule. One bot token is shared by every tenant.
pros: Setup was one form field, so a new tenant could connect Discord in a minute.
One shared bot is simpler to run than one bot per tenant.
cons: Tenant B could list up to 25,000 members of tenant A's server, with user names and nicknames.
Tenant B could import tenant A's custom emoji.
New sign-ins from tenant A's server silently got an account in tenant B too (migration 0113).
The Test Connection button told anyone which servers the bot had joined.

coas.name: Only the platform admin can bind a server
coas.description: Remove the server ID field from tenant settings. The platform admin sets it for each tenant by hand after checking ownership.
pros: No Discord code changes.
A person checks every binding.
cons: Every new tenant waits for the platform admin.
The check is manual, so it can be skipped or done wrong.

coas.name: Prove Manage Server through Discord sign-in
coas.description: Ask Discord which servers the signed-in admin can manage. Only allow a server they own or hold Manage Server on. Add a unique index so one server maps to one tenant.
pros: Tenants still set up Discord on their own.
Discord itself confirms who runs the server.
The database blocks two tenants from sharing a server, even if the code has a bug.
cons: The admin must have linked their Discord account first.
Adds a call to Discord and token refresh handling.
Needs a migration that fails if old data already has duplicates.
coas.recommendedReason: It closes the leak without making tenants wait for the platform admin.

coas.name: Do nothing
coas.description: Accept the risk because every tenant today is run by people who know each other.
pros: No work.
cons: The first tenant run by a stranger can read another group's member list.
Member names leak without anyone being told.

findings.title: Ten REST reads at once can freeze the whole web server
findings.summary: Each REST read holds one database connection and then asks for a second one from the same pool. With ten reads at once, every request in the process hangs, including sign-in.

evidence.note: The rate-limit check runs inside the tenant transaction, so connection 1 is still held.
`withRateLimit` takes connection 2 from the same shared pool.
The pool holds 10 connections by default.
No pool sets a checkout timeout. The `pg` default is to wait forever, so a full pool never recovers.
Writes take the rate-limit token inside the command transaction. If the request fails, the rollback gives the token back, so failed writes are never throttled.
This route does it the safe way: it checks the rate limit before it opens any transaction.

current.description: `handleRead` opens the tenant transaction first, then checks the rate limit on the shared pool. `handleMutation` checks the limit inside the write transaction. About nine routes skip these helpers and check the limit first.
pros: One helper wraps auth, the transaction and the rate limit, so most routes stay short.
The write limit and the write succeed or fail together, which is easy to reason about.
cons: Ten slow reads at once use every connection, and each waits for an eleventh that never comes. The process stops serving everyone.
Failed writes hand back their token, so someone probing the API is never slowed down.
The token row is locked for the whole write, so one user's writes run one at a time.
Routes disagree on where the check goes, so new routes copy whichever one they see first.

coas.name: Check the limit before the transaction
coas.description: In both helpers, take the rate-limit token in its own short transaction before opening the tenant transaction. Also set `connectionTimeoutMillis` on every pool so a full pool returns 503 instead of hanging.
pros: Removes the deadlock: a request never holds one connection while waiting for another.
Failed writes still spend their token, so probing is throttled.
Matches the routes that already do it right, so there is one pattern.
cons: A request that is later refused by a permission check still spends a token.
Touches the helper every API route uses, so it needs a careful test run.
coas.recommendedReason: It removes the cause, not just the symptom, and the safe pattern already exists in the codebase.

coas.name: Run the check on the tenant transaction
coas.description: Pass `tenantDb` into the rate-limit check so it uses connection 1 instead of asking for connection 2.
pros: Smallest change: one argument.
Removes the deadlock.
cons: Failed requests still give their token back.
The token row stays locked for the whole request, so a user's requests queue up.

coas.name: Only add a pool timeout
coas.description: Set `connectionTimeoutMillis` so a full pool fails fast. Leave the order of operations as it is.
pros: One-line change with no change to request logic.
The server recovers on its own instead of hanging until restart.
cons: Under load, users still get errors instead of pages.
Failed writes are still not throttled.

findings.title: Night theme hides links and active items in the tenant's brand colour
findings.summary: In the night theme, text drawn in the tenant's brand colour is dark navy on near-black. Night users cannot see wiki links, the active menu item or page eyebrows.

evidence.caption: Night theme, wiki page: links, the active sidebar item and the active table-of-contents item are navy on near-black.

evidence.note: The tenant's brand colour is used as-is for every theme. Nothing lightens it for night.
Page eyebrows use the raw brand colour for text.
The active table-of-contents item also uses the raw brand colour.
Night mode already mixes `--link-ink` toward the text colour. Only rules that use `--link-ink` get that help; the rules above do not.
A test pins the exact night `--link-ink` formula, so any change must update this test too.

current.description: Each tenant picks a brand colour. `tenantBrandStyle` writes it to `--squadron`, and many CSS rules use `--squadron` directly for text, borders and fills in both themes.
pros: The brand colour looks the same everywhere, which tenants asked for.
One variable is easy to reason about.
It works well in the day theme, where most brand colours are dark.
cons: Dark brand colours drop to about 2:1 contrast on the night background. The accessibility minimum for text is 4.5:1.
Every tenant with a dark brand colour is affected, and they cannot fix it themselves.
The fix for links in `foundation.css` does not reach eyebrows, the active menu item or the table of contents.

coas.name: Add a night text version of the brand colour
coas.description: Add a `--squadron-text` variable. In the night theme, lighten the brand colour until it reaches 4.5:1 contrast. Use it for every text rule that uses `--squadron` today.
pros: Keeps the tenant's colour, just lighter where it has to be read.
Works for every tenant with no action from them.
Borders and fills keep the exact brand colour.
cons: About 28 CSS rules must switch variables, and it is easy to miss one.
The lightened colour is close to the brand, not exact.
coas.recommendedReason: It fixes every tenant at once and keeps the brand look, for a moderate CSS change.

coas.name: Let tenants set a separate night colour
coas.description: Add a second colour field to unit branding and use it when the night theme is on.
pros: Tenants get full control over how their brand looks at night.
cons: Needs a database column, a form field and a migration.
Tenants who never set it stay broken.
Nothing stops a tenant from picking another dark colour.

coas.name: Stop using the brand colour for text
coas.description: Use the normal text colour for eyebrows, links and active items. Keep the brand colour only for borders, bars and fills.
pros: Always readable in both themes.
Simple rule for future CSS: brand colour is never text.
cons: Pages lose some brand colour in the day theme too.
Links need another cue, such as an underline, to stand out.

findings.title: Paged lists can repeat or skip rows
findings.summary: Some lists sort only by columns that can tie, such as join date or title. When users page through them, a row can show up twice or not at all.

evidence.note: The name sorts end on `id`, which makes the order stable.
Most other sorts stop at first name. Two members with the same name and join date can swap places.
Wiki page lists sort by `title` only and then use `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`.
The members API builds each page by slicing a fresh query, so it has the same problem.

current.description: List queries sort by what the user picked, then by name. Pages are cut with `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`. Postgres does not promise any order among rows that tie.
pros: The sort order matches what users expect to see.
The name sorts are already stable.
Most units are small, so ties across a page boundary are rare.
cons: When ties do cross a page boundary, a member can be missed during a review.
The bug is hard to reproduce, so a user report would be hard to confirm.

coas.name: Add `id` as the last sort key everywhere
coas.description: End every paged `ORDER BY` with the row's `id`, the way the name sorts already do.
pros: Small, mechanical change.
Order is fully stable, so pages never overlap.
cons: Must be remembered for every new paged query.
coas.recommendedReason: It fixes the bug for a few lines of change with almost no risk.

coas.name: Switch to cursor paging
coas.description: Page by "rows after this sort key and id" instead of by page number.
pros: Stable even when rows are added between page loads.
Faster on large tables.
cons: Changes the API contract and the UI's page controls.
Much more work than the bug is worth today.

coas.name: Do nothing
coas.description: Accept the risk because lists are small and ties are rare.
pros: No work.
cons: Rare, confusing bugs stay possible.

fixFirst.why: Ten REST reads at once can hang the whole web process, and failed writes are never throttled.
Night users cannot see links or where they are in the wiki.
Cross-tenant member list leak through a claimed Discord server. Fixed; kept here for the record.

openQuestions.text: Should tenants be able to set their own night colour later, even if we lighten it by default now?
What should a full pool return to users: a 503 page, or a retry after a short wait?

clean.text: Local invite and reset tokens, sign-in limits, the upload pipeline and public wiki grants hold up. All 27 permission keys are seeded.
Next 16 async APIs are used correctly. `redirect` and `notFound` are rethrown. RBAC (role-based access control) has no catch-to-allow paths.
The login page, units tree and wiki desktop read view look good in the day theme. The page never scrolls sideways.

notes: Example report for the audit-report tool. Evidence was checked against the working tree on 2026-09-26. SEC-03 line numbers point at the fixed code.
